statement: Resistor thermal noise voltage is V_R = sqrt(4kTBR), where k is Boltzmann's constant, T is absolute temperature, B is bandwidth and R is resistance.
A 1 kOhm resistor at 25 C has a thermal noise density of about 4.055 nV/sqrt(Hz); ESP rounds this to 4.1 nV/sqrt(Hz).
A 200 Ohm resistor at room temperature produces 257 nV of thermal noise over a 20 kHz bandwidth, corresponding to an EIN floor of -129.6 dBu.
A 100 Ohm resistor produces 182 nV over 20 kHz, 3 dB lower than a 200 Ohm resistor.
Independent noise voltages add in RMS quadrature: two equal 1 V sources sum to 1.414 V, and three 3 mV sources sum to about 5.2 mV.
locator: §1, paragraph 'Always remember that noise signals do not simply add'

statement: Voltage noise dominates at low source impedance and current noise at high source impedance; bipolar inputs suit roughly 1 kOhm to 10 kOhm sources and FET inputs suit roughly 10 kOhm to 100 kOhm sources.
An inverting stage at unity signal gain has a noise gain of 2 because the input and feedback resistors contribute, so low-noise designs usually use the non-inverting topology.
An op-amp with 5 nV/sqrt(Hz) input noise integrates to 707 nV over 20 kHz; at a gain of 100 this is 70.7 uV at the output, an input-referred -123 dBV, or 83 dB below 1 V.
An op-amp noise density in nV/sqrt(Hz) is converted to integrated noise by multiplying by the square root of the bandwidth; 5 nV/sqrt(Hz) times sqrt(20000) is about 707 nV.
Paralleling two identical devices reduces noise by 3 dB, four by 6 dB and eight by 9 dB; two to six devices is a practical compromise.
In ESP's measurement at 46 dB gain, a 1458 op-amp gave about 65 dB signal-to-noise ratio while an LM833 gave about 82 dB, close to the 83 dB theoretical best for a 200 Ohm source.
Resistor thermal noise rises by 3 dB per doubling of resistance, or 20 dB per factor of 100.
Over the normal equipment temperature range the effect on resistor noise is small: a 1 kOhm resistor changes from 4.07 nV/sqrt(Hz) at 29 C to 4.7 nV/sqrt(Hz) at 125 C, a 1.25 dB increase.
Thermal noise is modeled as e^2 = 4kTR df for voltage or i^2 = (4kT/R) df for current, with spectral densities in V^2/Hz and A^2/Hz.
A spectral density is a noise voltage or current per root hertz, in V/sqrt(Hz) or A/sqrt(Hz).
For a first-order low-pass response the equivalent noise bandwidth is 1.57 times the 3 dB bandwidth.
An op-amp noise model places a voltage noise source in series with one input and current noise sources at both inputs; independent resistor and device noise sources are combined by RMS summation.
In a non-inverting amplifier the noise gain is 1 + Rf/Rg, and each noise source is multiplied by its gain to the output before RMS summation.
Flicker noise has a 1/f spectral density and is specified by a corner frequency below which it dominates white noise.
Op-amp selection should consider circuit type, required speed, load drive, signal level, noise, supply voltage, package and cost; unsupported claims about 'sound' are not selection criteria.

ESP's compiled typical datasheet values include AD797 0.9 nV/sqrt(Hz), 110 MHz and 20 V/us; LT1115 0.9 nV/sqrt(Hz), 70 MHz and 15 V/us; OPA1612 1.1 nV/sqrt(Hz), 40 MHz and 27 V/us; LM4562 2.7 nV/sqrt(Hz), 55 MHz and 20 V/us; NE5532 5 nV/sqrt(Hz), 10 MHz and 9 V/us; TL072 18 nV/sqrt(Hz), 3 MHz and 13 V/us; and uA741 23 nV/sqrt(Hz), 1 MHz and 0.5 V/us.
A 1 kOhm ideal resistor has 4 nV/sqrt(Hz) noise, and about 1 kOhm is a fair estimate of the average output impedance of typical signal sources.
Driving a 600 Ohm load calls for an op-amp rated for the purpose, such as an NE5532/4, LM4562 or OPA2134; a high-impedance source calls for a JFET-input op-amp.
The JFET-input TL072 has higher voltage noise than bipolar audio op-amps but outperforms them with a high-impedance source.
A 741 with a 0.5 V/us slew rate can still deliver about 3 V RMS at 20 kHz, so slew rate must be checked against the required full-power bandwidth rather than assumed from the part's reputation.
Douglas Self measured NE5532/4 distortion below 0.0005% at all frequencies below 10 kHz with a 5 V RMS output on +/-18 V supplies.

Self identifies eight distortion mechanisms in a generic Class-B power amplifier: input stage, VAS, output stage (large-signal nonlinearity, crossover and switchoff), VAS loading, decoupling return and rail induction, feedback takeoff point, and capacitor nonlinearity.

Class-B crossover distortion occurs over a small part of the transfer characteristic, generates high-order harmonics, and is present at all output levels; the THD percentage can rise as output level falls.
At +/-40 V, Self's CFP output stage produced 0.014% THD at 8 Ohm and 0.030% at 4 Ohm, versus 0.031% and 0.042% for the emitter-follower stage.
In the same comparison a simple MOSFET output stage produced 0.47% THD at 8 Ohm and 0.84% at 4 Ohm, much worse than the BJT emitter-follower or CFP stages.
Large-signal nonlinearity increases as load impedance falls below 8 Ohm, and the third harmonic appears and dominates at low loads.
Output-device beta droop causes gain droop; paralleling two output devices reduces distortion by about 1.9 times, and sustained-beta devices reduce 4 Ohm distortion by about 1.4 times.

Optimal Class-B bias is set by the voltage between the output-device emitters, not by quiescent current alone; changing emitter resistors from 0.1 Ohm to 0.47 Ohm changes the optimal quiescent current but barely changes the required bias voltage.

An emitter-follower output stage can reverse-bias an output device's base-emitter junction during switchoff by about -0.5 V at 8 Ohm and -1.6 V at 4 Ohm; a 1 uF speed-up capacitor can halve THD at 40 kHz.
VAS loading distortion is caused by the nonlinear input impedance of the Class-B output stage; a VAS buffer or local feedback linearizes it.
Input-pair transconductance is greatest at zero differential input and is proportional to tail current; emitter degeneration linearizes the pair but reduces the available negative feedback factor.

Input-stage distortion rises at 12 dB/octave when the stage is unbalanced and 18 dB/octave when balanced, because the signal current needed to drive the dominant compensation capacitor doubles each octave while loop gain falls 6 dB/octave.
Self's 'Blameless' Class-B design achieves below 0.0005% THD at 1 kHz and 0.003% at 10 kHz.

A microphone preamplifier must provide low noise with low source impedance, high signal handling, RF immunity, high common-mode rejection, variable differential gain from 1 to 1000 or more, and usually +48 V phantom power.
Phantom-power faults can apply -48 V to a preamplifier input; protection requires series resistors, diode clamps and capacitors that absorb charge.

A 20 dB balanced U-pad can keep the input impedance near 2 kOhm and reduce resistor matching errors; a bipolar-input preamplifier should see a differential source impedance no higher than about 2 kOhm.
RF immunity is improved by capacitors at the input connector returned to the connector shield, plus a third capacitor to shunt differential RF inside the enclosure.
Phantom feed resistors should be thin film, matched to 1% or better, and rated for the shorted-input dissipation of 0.338 W each.
With +/-15 V supplies the THAT 1570 accepts at least +26.8 dBu differential input at unity gain without clipping.
EIN is measured at maximum gain with the input terminated by the expected source impedance; the standard source impedance is 150 Ohm.

A 150 Ohm source at room temperature has a thermal-noise limit of -131 dBu over 20 kHz and -134 dBu over 10 kHz; noise falls by 3 dB when the bandwidth is halved because voltage is a square-root function.

Self measured that a 2% input-pair collector-current imbalance raised THD from 0.10% to 0.16% at -45 dBu, and a 10% imbalance raised it to 0.55%; balance should be within 1% for lowest high-frequency distortion.
Self notes that capacitor distortion is usually Distortion 8, and that it can be distinguished from Distortion 5 because Distortion 5 typically rises by only 6 dB/octave.
